intro: A low rumble shoots to the top of the piano; the reply is quiet and languid. Scriabin’s Fifth Sonata keeps both characters in a single movement, driving its soft opening song towards a triple-forte climax.

cues.title: From the bottom of the piano
cues.text: A trill and rumbling left hand send a rush of notes upwards. A pause clears the keyboard for Languido: soft, sweet chords and a melody marked con voglia, with desire. The sonata begins with two kinds of motion.
cues.evidence: Author’s edition, engraved by C. G. Röder, pp. 2–3: Allegro impetuoso con stravaganza, Presto, a fermata, then Languido, pp dolcissimo and con voglia. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/30620
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Joy, off the beat
cues.text: Presto con allegrezza — very fast, with joy — gives the sonata its skipping main theme. The right-hand chords fall against the left hand’s leaping accompaniment, making the phrase bounce across the beat.
cues.evidence: Author’s edition, p. 4, the Presto con allegrezza theme. Gerald Larner identifies its syncopation and its role as the main subject. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/30620; https://geraldlarner.com/work/scriabin-piano-sonata-no-5-in-f-sharp-major-op-53-1907
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Meno vivo
cues.text: The slower Meno vivo brings another melody, marked accarezzevole: caressingly. Chromatic inner voices move beneath it. This quiet idea will acquire a much louder, more forceful character in the development.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner describes the Meno vivo theme, its accarezzevole marking, chromatic counterpoint and climactic treatment in the development. https://geraldlarner.com/work/scriabin-piano-sonata-no-5-in-f-sharp-major-op-53-1907
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One movement from now on
cues.text: Written in 1907, the Fifth is Scriabin’s first numbered piano sonata in a single movement. He keeps that form for all five that follow. The slow, fast and ecstatic passages now have to belong to one continuous span.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner gives the date, one-movement form and its continuation in Sonatas Nos. 6–10. The preceding four sonatas have more than one movement; the Fifth is identified as the first single-movement sonata in the work history. https://geraldlarner.com/work/scriabin-piano-sonata-no-5-in-f-sharp-major-op-53-1907; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._5_(Scriabin)

cues.title: The composer’s own epigraph
cues.text: Above the first bar Scriabin prints lines from his own Poem of Ecstasy: “I call you to life, O mysterious forces!” The words summon timid beginnings of life from the dark depths of the creative spirit.
cues.evidence: Author’s edition, p. 2, prints the epigraph in French and Russian. The quoted first line translates “Je vous appelle à la vie, ô forces mystérieuses!”; the remaining description follows the next three lines. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/30620

cues.title: The dance comes back
cues.text: After the development’s increasingly forceful treatment of the themes, the skipping Presto returns. The sonata revisits its earlier ideas before a final expansion of the quiet melody from the introduction.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner describes the development’s climax, the recapitulation of the exposition’s themes, and the subsequent enlargement of the introductory con voglia theme. https://geraldlarner.com/work/scriabin-piano-sonata-no-5-in-f-sharp-major-op-53-1907
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Estatico at full force
cues.text: The soft introductory song reaches estatico and triple forte, high above repeated chords. Scriabin crowns it in E♭ major rather than the sonata’s F♯. The last page releases another upward rush and stops without a settling final chord.
cues.evidence: Author’s edition, p. 19: estatico, fff, E-flat-major harmony, then the introductory rushing figure and a final rest. Gerald Larner describes the displaced tonal climax and unanchored ending. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/30620; https://geraldlarner.com/work/scriabin-piano-sonata-no-5-in-f-sharp-major-op-53-1907
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: He wrote a part for coloured light that had to be omitted at the work’s first performance.
facts: Moscow Conservatory, 1888–92: Safonov, Taneyev and Arensky
Piano professor at the Moscow Conservatory from 1898
Publisher Mitrofan Belyayev; conductor Serge Koussevitzky
Ten piano sonatas; three symphonies; a concerto; The Poem of Ecstasy and Prometheus
composer.background:
At the Moscow première of Prometheus in 1911, Scriabin sat at the piano and Serge Koussevitzky conducted. The audience heard the huge orchestra, the solo piano and the harmonies which seem to hang in the air before the first horn melody. One part of the score remained silent and invisible: the keyboard intended to project coloured light. Alexander Mozer had built a small apparatus for Scriabin, but Scriabin withdrew it from the concert because of technical difficulties. The lights were dropped. Scriabin had written for an instrument the concert hall could scarcely accommodate.

He was born in Moscow in 1872. His mother, Lyubov, was a trained pianist; she died when he was a baby. With his father pursuing a diplomatic career abroad, his aunt, also Lyubov, helped bring him up. He entered the cadet corps in 1882, took lessons from Nikolai Zverev, and joined Vasily Safonov’s piano class at the Moscow Conservatory in 1888. Rachmaninoff studied there too. Scriabin graduated as a pianist in 1892, a year after Rachmaninoff, but left without completing the composition course with Sergei Taneyev and Anton Arensky.
